questions.question: ¿Cuál es el vector biológico de Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti es transmitida principalmente por mosquitos Culex quinquefasciatus en áreas urbanas, aunque también pueden actuar como vectores especies de Anopheles y Aedes en diferentes regiones geográficas.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la microfilaremia característica de Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti presenta periodicidad nocturna, las microfilarias aparecen en sangre periférica durante la noche, coincidiendo con el hábito de alimentación del mosquito vector, lo que facilita su transmisión.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la forma infectante para el ser humano?
questions.explanation: La larva filariforme L3 es la forma infectante que el mosquito deposita en la piel del hospedero humano durante la picadura; luego migra al sistema linfático donde madura a adulto.

questions.question: ¿Dónde se localizan los gusanos adultos de Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Los gusanos adultos de Wuchereria bancrofti habitan en los vasos y ganglios linfáticos, causando obstrucción linfática crónica que conduce a linfedema y elefantiasis en extremidades y genitales.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de elección para la filariasis linfática?
questions.explanation: La dietilcarbamazina (DEC) es el fármaco de elección para la filariasis linfática por Wuchereria bancrofti, ya que elimina microfilarias y tiene efecto parcial sobre los gusanos adultos; se usa en combinación con albendazol en programas de eliminación.

questions.question: ¿Qué reacción adversa es característica del tratamiento con dietilcarbamazina?
questions.explanation: El síndrome de Mazzotti ocurre por la destrucción masiva de microfilarias tras la administración de dietilcarbamazina, manifestándose con fiebre, cefalea, mialgias y prurito, especialmente en pacientes con alta carga parasitaria.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el principal vector de la filariasis linfática en áreas urbanas?
questions.explanation: El mosquito Culex quinquefasciatus es el vector urbano más importante de Wuchereria bancrofti, especialmente en zonas con aguas contaminadas, siendo clave en la transmisión de la filariasis linfática.

questions.question: ¿Qué especie parasitaria transmite principalmente el mosquito Culex?
questions.explanation: Culex is a vector of Wuchereria bancrofti, the most common cause of lymphatic filariasis; Brugia malayi is transmitted by Mansonia and Anopheles, while Onchocerca and Loa have other vectors.

questions.question: ¿Qué característica del Culex favorece la transmisión urbana de filariasis?
questions.explanation: El Culex se cría en aguas estancadas y contaminadas, comunes en áreas urbanas con saneamiento deficiente, lo que facilita su proliferación y la transmisión de Wuchereria bancrofti en estas zonas.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el horario de picadura típico del Culex transmisor de filariasis?
questions.explanation: El Culex tiene actividad picadora nocturna, lo que coincide con la microfilaremia nocturna de Wuchereria bancrofti, facilitando la transmisión durante el sueño del hospedero.

questions.question: ¿Qué medida es más efectiva para controlar el vector Culex en zonas urbanas?
questions.explanation: La eliminación de criaderos (aguas estancadas) es la medida más efectiva contra Culex, ya que reduce la población vectorial y la transmisión; los mosquiteros diurnos no aplican y no existe vacuna.

questions.question: ¿Qué fase del parásito es infectante para el mosquito Culex?
questions.explanation: Las microfilarias son ingeridas por el Culex al picar a un infectado; dentro del mosquito se desarrollan hasta larva L3, que es la fase infectante para el humano, no para el vector.

questions.question: ¿Cuál de los siguientes parásitos produce microfilarias con vaina?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti produce microfilarias con vaina, al igual que Brugia malayi y Loa loa. Mansonella perstans y Onchocerca volvulus producen microfilarias sin vaina.

questions.question: ¿Qué característica morfológica distingue a las microfilarias de Wuchereria bancrofti?
options: Cuerpo corto y curvado en forma de cayado
Núcleos que llegan hasta la punta caudal
Ausencia de núcleos en extremo caudal
Presencia de vaina y cola puntiaguda
questions.explanation: Las microfilarias de Wuchereria bancrofti presentan vaina, cola puntiaguda y núcleos que no llegan al extremo caudal. Esta característica permite diferenciarlas de Brugia, cuyo extremo caudal tiene núcleos.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el periodo de aparición en sangre periférica de las microfilarias de Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti presenta periodicidad nocturna, con pico de microfilaremia entre las 22:00 y 2:00 horas, lo que condiciona la toma de muestra sanguínea a esa hora para el diagnóstico.

questions.question: ¿Qué técnica de diagnóstico se utiliza para observar microfilarias con vaina?
options: Frotis de sangre periférica teñido con Giemsa
Cultivo en medio de agar sangre
questions.explanation: El frotis de sangre periférica teñido con Giemsa permite visualizar microfilarias, incluyendo la vaina. La biopsia de piel se usa para Onchocerca, la orina para Schistosoma y el cultivo no es útil para filarias.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de elección para la filariasis linfática por Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: La dietilcarbamazina (DEC) es el fármaco de elección para la filariasis linfática, ya que elimina las microfilarias y tiene efecto sobre los adultos. La ivermectina se usa en oncocercosis y la albendazol como complemento.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el vector biológico que transmite Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti es transmitida principalmente por mosquitos Culex quinquefasciatus en áreas urbanas, aunque también por Anopheles y Aedes. Simulium transmite Onchocerca y Culicoides transmite Mansonella.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el principal mecanismo que explica la periodicidad nocturna de Wuchereria bancrofti?
options: Relación con el ciclo circadiano del huésped
Adaptación a la presión parcial de oxígeno
questions.explanation: The nocturnal periodicity of Wuchereria bancrofti is related to the host's circadian cycle, since microfilariae appear in peripheral blood at night, when the mosquito vector has greater feeding activity, facilitating transmission.

questions.question: ¿Qué especie de filaria presenta periodicidad nocturna en regiones endémicas?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti is the filaria that has a nocturnal periodicity in most endemic regions, unlike Loa loa which is diurnal. Brugia malayi and timori can also be nocturnal, but the question focuses on the most representative species.

questions.question: What is the typical time of highest concentration of microfilariae in peripheral blood in nocturnal filariasis?
options: Between 2 p.m. m. and 6 p.m. m.
Between 4 a.m. m. and 8 a.m. m.
Between 6 a.m. m. and 12 p.m. m.
Between 10 p.m. m. and 2 a. m.
questions.explanation: In nocturnal filariasis, microfilariae reach their maximum peak in peripheral blood between 10 p.m. m. and 2 a. m., coinciding with the bite time of the vector mosquito, which optimizes transmission.

questions.question: What diagnostic method requires considering nocturnal periodicity to increase its sensitivity?
questions.explanation: The thick peripheral blood smear is the classic method to detect microfilariae, and its sensitivity depends on the time of collection; It should be performed at night to capture the highest concentration of microfilariae in the blood.

questions.question: What is the main clinical implication of nocturnal periodicity in the diagnosis of filariasis?
options: Requires blood draw during the day
The sample must be taken on an empty stomach
questions.explanation: La periodicidad nocturna obliga a que la extracción de sangre para el diagnóstico parasitológico se realice durante la noche, cuando las microfilarias circulan en sangre periférica; de lo contrario, el resultado puede ser falso negativo.

questions.question: ¿Qué factor se asocia a la aparición de microfilarias en sangre periférica durante la noche?
questions.explanation: Nocturnal periodicity has been related to host melatonin levels, which increase during the night and could influence the migration of microfilariae to the peripheral blood, synchronized with the circadian cycle.

questions.question: What is the reference method for the diagnosis of lymphatic filariasis in the acute phase?
questions.explanation: The thick smear is the classic and reference parasitological method to detect microfilariae in peripheral blood, especially in lymphatic filariasis, although its sensitivity depends on the periodicity of the microfilariae.

questions.question: What stain is used to visualize microfilariae in the thick smear?
questions.explanation: Giemsa stain is the most used to stain microfilariae in smears and thick smears, allowing us to observe their morphology and differentiate species. The other stains are not suitable for blood parasites.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of thick smear for diagnosing lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: The thick smear has low sensitivity when the density of microfilariae is low, as occurs in chronic infections or in asymptomatic carriers, which can generate false negatives and requires repeated samples.

questions.question: At what time is it recommended to take the sample for thick smears in filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti has a nocturnal frequency, so blood collection for thick smears should be carried out between 10 and 2 hours, when the concentration of microfilariae in peripheral blood is maximum.

questions.question: What species of filaria has a diurnal periodicity and is diagnosed with a thick blood drop taken at midday?
questions.explanation: Loa loa presents microfilariae with a diurnal period, so the thick smear must be obtained around noon. The other species have nocturnal periodicity or are not diagnosed by thick smear.

questions.question: What alternative to thick smear is used when there is clinical suspicion but negative microfilaremia?
questions.explanation: The circulating antigen test (such as ICT card test) is more sensitive than the thick smear and does not depend on periodicity, being useful in cases with low or absent microfilaremia, such as chronic filariasis.

questions.question: What is the main use of the rapid antigen test in lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: The rapid antigen test (ICT) detects Wuchereria bancrofti antigens in blood, being useful for diagnosing active infection even without microfilaremia.

questions.question: What species of filaria is detected with the rapid antigen test?
questions.explanation: The rapid antigen test is designed specifically to detect Wuchereria bancrofti, not other filariae such as Brugia or Onchocerca.

questions.question: What is an advantage of the rapid antigen test over the thick smear?
options: Does not require a blood sample
questions.explanation: The antigen test can detect infection in patients with low or absent microfilaremia, overcoming the limitation of the thick smear that depends on the presence of microfilariae.

questions.question: At what time of day is it recommended to perform the rapid test?
questions.explanation: Unlike the thick smear that requires a night sample due to the periodicity of the microfilariae, the rapid antigen test can be performed at any time.

questions.question: What result does the rapid test indicate in a patient with elephantiasis?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic elephantiasis, the antigen test may be negative if the active infection has disappeared, since the pathology is secondary to previous lymphatic damage.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of the rapid antigen test?
options: It only works on venous blood
questions.explanation: The test does not distinguish between active infection and previous exposure, so in endemic areas there may be residual positivity after successful treatment.

questions.question: What structure is observed in motion during the filarial dance sign?
questions.explanation: The filarial dance sign is an ultrasonographic finding that shows rapid, erratic movements of live adult worms within dilated lymphatic vessels, typical of chronic lymphatic filariasis.

questions.question: What species of filaria is most frequently associated with the filarial dance sign?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti es el principal agente causal de filariasis linfática a nivel mundial, y su presencia en vasos linfáticos produce el característico signo ultrasonográfico de danza filarial.

questions.question: ¿En qué tipo de vasos se visualiza típicamente el signo de danza filarial?
questions.explanation: Los gusanos adultos de Wuchereria bancrofti habitan y obstruyen los vasos linfáticos, causando dilatación proximal. El ultrasonido en estos vasos linfáticos dilatados revela el movimiento activo de los parásitos.

questions.question: What is the main usefulness of the filarial dance sign in clinical practice?
questions.explanation: Visualization of the filarial dance sign allows confirmation of the presence of live adult worms, which indicates active infection and guides the decision to initiate antifilarial treatment, unlike the detection of antigens alone.

questions.question: What clinical finding correlates with the presence of the filarial dance sign?
questions.explanation: The filarial dance sign is observed in patients with lymphatic filariasis who present chronic manifestations such as lymphoedema or elephantiasis, reflecting lymphatic obstruction caused by adult parasites.

questions.question: What treatment is indicated when the filarial dance sign is detected?
questions.explanation: The diethylcarbamazine (DEC) diet combined with albendazole is the standard treatment for active lymphatic filariasis, aimed at eliminating microfilariae and reducing the adult worm burden.

questions.question: What is the most common etiological agent of lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti is the parasite responsible for approximately 90% of lymphatic filariasis cases worldwide, transmitted by Culex, Anopheles and Aedes mosquitoes, and causes chronic lymphedema of the extremities.

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanism contributes to the development of lymphedema in filariasis?
questions.explanation: Adult parasites lodge in lymphatic vessels and cause mechanical obstruction, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, which impedes lymphatic drainage and leads to irreversible lymphedema in the lower extremities.

questions.question: What is the diagnostic method of choice in acute lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Detection of circulating antigens of Wuchereria bancrofti by immunochromatographic test is the diagnostic standard in the acute phase, since microfilaraemia can be intermittent and biopsy is not recommended due to the risk of worsening lymphedema.

questions.question: What is the recommended drug treatment for lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: La combinación de dietilcarbamazina y albendazol es el tratamiento de elección para la filariasis linfática por Wuchereria bancrofti, ya que elimina microfilarias y tiene efecto parcial sobre parásitos adultos, reduciendo la transmisión.

questions.question: ¿Qué complicación aguda característica se presenta en pacientes con filariasis linfática?
questions.explanation: Acute adenolymphangitis is a recurrent febrile complication caused by the death of adult parasites or secondary bacterial infection, manifesting with painful inflammation of lymph nodes and vessels, which accelerates the progression of lymphedema.

questions.question: At what clinical stage of filariasis lymphedema is fibrosis and dermal warts observed?
questions.explanation: Stage III (elephantiasis) is characterized by massive increase in the volume of the limb, thickened skin with fibrosis, warts and deep folds, as well as irreversible deformity that limits mobility and predisposes to recurrent bacterial infections.

questions.question: What is the main cause of elephantiasis in lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti is the most common etiological agent of lymphatic filariasis, causing elephantiasis due to chronic lymphatic obstruction. Onchocerca causes onchocerciasis, Loa loa causes loiasis and Dracunculus causes dracunculiasis, all clinically different.

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanism leads to hydrocele in filariasis?
questions.explanation: In lymphatic filariasis, obstruction of the lymphatic vessels of the spermatic cord and scrotum by adult parasites causes fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis, producing hydrocele. The other options are not primary mechanisms in this disease.

questions.question: What is the drug of choice to treat lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the treatment of choice for lymphatic filariasis, since it eliminates microfilariae and has an effect on adults. Ivermectin is used in onchocerciasis and strongyloidiasis, albendazole in intestinal helminthiasis and praziquantel in trematodes and cestodes.

questions.question: What clinical finding distinguishes filarial hydrocele from nonfilarial hydrocele?
questions.explanation: Filarial hydrocele may contain chylous fluid due to lymphatic obstruction, a characteristic finding that differentiates it from hydroceles of other etiology. Increased volume is common to both, acute pain is not typical and thickening of the cord can be seen in other pathologies.

questions.question: What is the standard parasitological diagnostic method for filariasis?
questions.explanation: Thick peripheral blood film taken at night is the standard method to detect Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae, taking advantage of its nocturnal periodicity. Skin biopsy is used for onchocerciasis, sputum culture is not useful, and serology has limitations.

questions.question: What chronic complication is unique to genital elephantiasis?
questions.explanation: Giant hydrocele is a characteristic chronic complication of genital elephantiasis, caused by massive lymphatic obstruction. Renal failure, hepatomegaly, and chylous ascites are not specific complications of genital elephantiasis.

questions.question: What is the main mechanism of action of diethylcarbamazine in lymphatic filariasis?
options: Alters the neuromuscular activity of the parasite
questions.explanation: Diethylcarbamazine acts by sensitizing microfilariae to the host's immune system and altering their neuromuscular activity, which facilitates their elimination by the host's defense mechanisms.

questions.question: What characteristic adverse effect is associated with treatment with diethylcarbamazine in patients with high microfilaremia?
questions.explanation: The Mazzotti reaction is a systemic reaction mediated by the release of antigens from dead microfilariae, manifesting with fever, myalgia, headache and pruritus, especially in patients with a high parasite load.

questions.question: What is the usual dose of diethylcarbamazine for the treatment of lymphatic filariasis in adults?
questions.explanation: The standard dose of diethylcarbamazine is 6 mg/kg/day divided into three doses, administered for 12 consecutive days, although alternative single-dose schedules exist in mass administration programs.

questions.question: In which of the following situations is diethylcarbamazine contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Diethylcarbamazine is contraindicated in pregnancy, as well as in patients with loiasis with high microfilaremia, due to the risk of severe encephalopathy. The other conditions do not contraindicate its use.

questions.question: What drug is used as an alternative when diethylcarbamazine is not available?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin is an effective alternative against Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae, although it is not as effective against adult parasites. Albendazole is used in combination, but not as monotherapy.

questions.question: What precaution should be taken before administering diethylcarbamazine in a patient from a loiasis endemic area?
options: Evaluate load of Loa loa microfilariae
questions.explanation: In patients with loiasis and high microfilaremia, diethylcarbamazine can cause severe encephalopathy; Therefore, it is recommended to evaluate the presence of Loa loa microfilariae before starting treatment.

questions.question: What is the main mechanism of action of ivermectin in lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Ivermectin binds to glutamate- and GABA-dependent chloride channels in parasites, increasing chloride influx, hyperpolarizing the cell, and causing neuromuscular paralysis of the microfilarium.

questions.question: What pharmacological effect does albendazole have on microfilariae?
options: Inhibits the synthesis of folic acid
questions.explanation: Albendazole is a benzimidazole that binds to the beta-tubulin of the parasite, inhibiting its polymerization and altering microtubules, which interrupts glucose uptake and depletes glycogen, causing the death of the microfilarium.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of combining ivermectin and albendazole in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis?
options: They do not require repeated doses
questions.explanation: The combination of ivermectin and albendazole is synergistic in reducing microfilaremia, since ivermectin quickly eliminates circulating microfilariae while albendazole acts more slowly and sustainably on the adult forms, improving therapeutic efficacy.

questions.question: What adverse effect is expected when treating patients with a high microfilarial load with ivermectin?
questions.explanation: The Mazzotti reaction occurs due to the massive death of microfilariae, releasing antigens that trigger an inflammatory response with fever, pruritus, myalgia and lymphadenopathy, especially in patients with a high parasite load.

questions.question: What limitation does ivermectin have in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis?
options: Does not penetrate the lymphatic system
questions.explanation: Ivermectin is very effective against circulating microfilariae but has little activity against adult worms located in the lymphatic vessels, so it is combined with albendazole to achieve a greater reduction in the adult burden.

questions.question: What is the standard dose of albendazole in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis in adults?
questions.explanation: The standard dose of albendazole for lymphatic filariasis is 400 mg as a single annual dose, administered together with ivermectin (150-200 µg/kg), as part of the mass drug administration strategy recommended by the WHO.

questions.question: What is the drug of choice in massive chemoprophylaxis against lymphatic filariasis?
questions.explanation: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the main drug in mass administration of drugs for lymphatic filariasis, frequently combined with albendazole or ivermectin to interrupt transmission.

questions.question: What annual schedule is recommended for the interruption of transmission in endemic areas?
options: Single annual dose of DEC plus albendazole
questions.explanation: The WHO strategy consists of administering a single annual dose of DEC plus albendazole in areas without onchocerciasis, managing to reduce microfilaremia and break the transmission cycle.

questions.question: In areas with onchocerciasis, what drug replaces DEC in mass treatment?
questions.explanation: In regions with onchocerciasis, DEC is contraindicated due to the risk of serious adverse reactions; Ivermectin is used, which is safe and effective against Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae.

questions.question: What is the main objective of mass drug administration in filariasis?
questions.explanation: Mass administration seeks to reduce microfilaremia in the population to cut transmission by mosquitoes, since current drugs have limited effect on adult worms.

questions.question: What strategy is used in areas where DEC is not available?
questions.explanation: When DEC is not available, the WHO recommends the combination of ivermectin and albendazole, which has demonstrated efficacy in reducing microfilaremia and is a validated alternative.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el efecto principal de la doxiciclina en la filariasis linfática?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline acts by eliminating Wolbachia, an endosymbiotic bacteria essential for the fertility and viability of the parasites, causing their gradual death; It is used in long-term regimens, not in annual mass administration.
